snip.t: Kidney (glomerulus & tubules): Filtration pressure, sodium handling, tubuloglomerular feedback — Hypertensive nephrosclerosis and secondary causes (renal artery stenosis, glomerulonephritis) alter this feedback, perpetuating hypertension
Renal artery stenosis: Abdominal bruit, flash pulmonary oedema, creatinine rise on ACE inhibitor; Doppler or CT angiography
ACEIs/ARBs: Contraindicated in pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, and severe hyperkalaemia.
Contra‑indications / safety: • ACE‑I/ARB in bilateral renal artery stenosis → stop if creatinine rises >30 % — • NSAIDs – avoid; they reduce renal perfusion
ACEI/ARB contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis, pregnancy, or severe hyperkalaemia.

qs.q: What is the gold standard investigation used to diagnose renal artery stenosis?
qs.e: Intra-arterial digital subtraction angiography (catheter angiography) is the gold standard renal arteriogram used for diagnosing renal artery stenosis. Renal duplex ultrasonography is used as a first-line test rather than the gold standard.

qs.q: A 65-year-old male smoker with diabetes is found to have renovascular hypertension. What is the most common underlying pathological cause of main renal artery stenosis in this patient demographic?
o: Uncontrolled complement activation due to a lack of regulatory proteins
Fibromuscular thickening involving the media and adventitia of the renal artery
Concentric atherosclerotic plaque formation at the origin of the renal artery
Endothelial injury secondary to Shiga-like toxin from bacterial enteritis
qs.e: Atherosclerotic plaque accounts for 70% of renal artery stenosis cases and is more common in older men and diabetics. Fibromuscular dysplasia typically affects younger women rather than older male smokers.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman is diagnosed with renal artery stenosis due to fibromuscular dysplasia. How do the internal arterioles of the ischemic kidney typically appear compared to the contralateral kidney?
o: Obstructed by large von Willebrand factor multimers and microthrombi
Exposed to full systemic hypertension, showing severe medial thickening
Completely obliterated by hyaline arteriolosclerosis and interstitial fibrosis
Protected from high pressure, showing only mild arteriolosclerosis
qs.e: The stenosis shields the downstream kidney from full systemic pressure, so its internal arterioles show only mild arteriolosclerosis while the opposite kidney suffers severe changes. The contralateral kidney is the one exposed to the full force of high pressure.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A patient experiences a sudden and complete blockage of a renal artery branch, leading to flank pain and hematuria. Gross pathological examination of the affected kidney tissue reveals which characteristic shape of infarction?
o: Wedge-shaped area of dead necrotic tissue
Ischemic atrophy confined to the medulla
qs.e: Renal infarcts caused by complete branch blockage present as characteristic wedge-shaped infarcts on imaging and at autopsy. A granular surface is characteristic of chronic nephrosclerosis rather than an acute infarct.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with a history of generalized atherosclerosis and progressive renal failure undergoes renal duplex ultrasonography, which reveals diffuse, bilateral luminal narrowing of the main renal vessels. Which of the following best characterizes this presentation compared to typical unilateral renal artery stenosis?
qs.e: Atherosclerotic ischemic renal disease typically involves bilateral, slowly progressive narrowing leading to chronic renal failure. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a distinct cause of renal artery stenosis that primarily affects younger females rather than causing this bilateral atherosclerotic pattern.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old male presents with newly diagnosed hypertension found to be caused by renal artery stenosis. What percentage of all hypertension cases are attributed to this specific renovascular condition?
qs.e: Renal artery stenosis is responsible for 2 to 5 percent of all hypertension cases and represents a curable cause. Higher percentages incorrectly overestimate the known prevalence of this specific condition.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: When a main renal artery becomes narrowed, the affected kidney experiences decreased blood flow and interprets this as a drop in systemic blood pressure. Which specific structure detects this low perfusion to release renin?
qs.e: The juxtaglomerular apparatus detects low perfusion and releases renin to activate the renin-angiotensin system. Mesangial cells provide structural support and phagocytosis rather than primary renin release.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

qs.q: A 35-year-old female is diagnosed with renal artery stenosis resulting from fibromuscular dysplasia. Which demographic and vessel layer feature distinguishes this pathology from atherosclerosis?
o: Concentric calcified plaque in older males
Thrombotic microthrombi caused by Shiga-like toxin
Fibrous thickening of the vessel wall in younger women
qs.e: Fibromuscular dysplasia involves fibrous thickening of the vessel wall and is more common in younger women in their 30s and 40s without atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is characteristically found in older males.
qs.s: Renal Vascular Diseases: Nephrosclerosis & Renal Artery Stenosis: MCQs

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The renal arteries are paired vessels that arise from the abdominal aorta and supply each kidney. Their course, branches, and relations are key to understanding renal perfusion, hypertension, and surgical approaches.

sections.p: Each kidney receives blood from a single renal artery that originates just below the superior mesenteric artery. The artery divides into segmental branches that follow the renal capsule.
The renal artery emerges from the lateral aspect of the abdominal aorta at the level of L1‑L2, passes posterior to the inferior vena cava (right side) or aorta (left), and enters the renal hilum.
On the right, the artery lies posterior to the inferior vena cava; on the left, it is anterior to the aorta. It is accompanied by the renal vein and ureter in the hilum.
b: At risk during aortic aneurysm repair

sections.p: After entering the hilum, the artery branches into anterior and posterior segmental arteries, which further divide into interlobar, arcuate, and interlobular arteries delivering blood to nephrons.
b: Segmental arteries are end‑arteries – no collateral flow
Ischemia of a segment causes focal infarction

sections.p: Sympathetic fibers travel with the renal artery from the thoracic splanchnic nerves, influencing renal vascular tone and renin release.
Delivers oxygenated blood to glomeruli, establishing the filtration pressure needed for urine formation and enabling renal autoregulation of flow and pressure.

Renal artery pathology can cause hypertension, renal insufficiency, or infarction. Common causes differ by setting: atherosclerosis in older adults, fibromuscular dysplasia in young women, and thrombosis or vasculitis in low‑resource regions.
b: Renal artery stenosis (RAS): 2‑5 % of hypertension; atheroma >70 % in older men, fibromuscular dysplasia in younger women
Thrombotic occlusion: seen with antiphospholipid syndrome, sickle cell, or severe dehydration
Vasculitis (e.g., polyarteritis nodosa, Takayasu) more common where infections like hepatitis B are prevalent

t.b: Detects velocity elevation → suggests stenosis; if unavailable, use captopril renography or clinical response to ACE‑I
Visualizes focal narrowing or beading; essential for planning revascularisation
Elevated in unilateral RAS; helps differentiate from bilateral disease

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: origin, course, segmental branches, common causes of stenosis, and the classic triad of abdominal bruit, flash pulmonary edema, and rise in creatinine after ACE‑I.
b: Goldblatt kidney: unilateral stenosis → renin‑driven hypertension
Bilateral gradual stenosis → slower rise in blood pressure, often missed

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden flank pain with hematuria (possible renal infarction)
Rapid rise in blood pressure with pulmonary edema after starting ACE‑I (suggests bilateral RAS)
Unexplained acute kidney injury with abdominal bruit

faq.q: Why does renal artery stenosis cause hypertension?
faq.a: Reduced perfusion triggers renin release, activating the angiotensin‑II cascade, which raises systemic blood pressure.

faq.q: How is fibromuscular dysplasia different from atherosclerotic RAS?
faq.a: FMD occurs in young women, shows a ‘string‑of‑beads’ appearance, and involves medial hyperplasia, while atherosclerosis affects older men with focal plaque.

faq.q: Can renal artery disease be cured?
faq.a: Yes, revascularisation (angioplasty ± stent for atherosclerotic lesions, balloon angioplasty for FMD) can restore flow and improve blood pressure in selected patients.

exam: Describe the origin, course, and segmental branching pattern of the renal artery.
Explain the pathophysiological mechanism linking unilateral renal artery stenosis to secondary hypertension.
List the major causes of renal artery stenosis and indicate which are most common in low‑resource settings.
